problem: Prior zero-shot object and room navigation systems (VLFM, ConceptGraphs, HOV-SG, Clio, SayPlan, SayNav, MoMa-LLM) are mostly confined to simulation or have other deployment gaps. Some assume perfect perception or localization (known poses, GT semantic masks), and some need pre-built scene graphs or offline processing. Others rely on dense representations that are too heavy for onboard compute, or on proprietary localization and navigation modules, so they are not end-to-end on a real robot.
motivation: Real-world deployment exposes problems that simulation abstracts away: imperfect perception, partial observability, localization drift, and safety constraints. Handling them needs three things working together in real time on onboard compute: reliable onboard SLAM, a planner that adapts online as the map changes, and a safe low-level controller. The authors observe that sparse, object-as-point hierarchical scene graphs are lightweight enough to build on a Jetson. Serialized as JSON, they give an LLM enough structured context to plan room-level search strategies.
key_idea: Build an open-source, modular, ROS2-based stack that runs almost entirely onboard a Unitree Go2. It incrementally builds an open-vocabulary hierarchical scene graph (rooms → objects) from 2D LiDAR SLAM plus an FP16-optimized FC-CLIP. A cloud GPT-4-Turbo planner iteratively picks high-level primitives (goto / search_room / explore_globally) over this graph, and the primitives are executed by Nav2 A*+MPPI with a CBF-QP safety filter.
insight:
Room-level abstraction is the component that matters for planning efficiency. In the dynamic-environment study (object introduced after mapping, 9 trials) the ablations compare as follows:
- Frontier-Search (no semantics) succeeds in 1/9.
- Object-Map-Search (object map, no room labels) reaches about 56%, because it misguesses where objects are, e.g., it goes to the nearest table in a break room to find a monitor.
- Full OrionNav with the hierarchical scene graph succeeds in 9/9 with generally lower completion times.
The failure breakdown over 96 real trials shows none of the 11 failures came from the LLM planner or scene graph. Instead they came from SLAM/odometry (3), frontier exploration (3), segmentation (4) and the CBF controller (1), so in the real world perception and localization, not reasoning, are the bottleneck. The VLFM analysis supports this: its HM3D SR drops from 52.5% to 42.3% under injected localization noise, and its dense map slows quadratically with map size (0.9 Hz → 0.5 Hz at 2.5× size, 0.17 Hz at 5×). Sim-trained dense-map methods therefore transfer poorly to the real world.
method: Open-vocabulary segmentation: FC-CLIP with a frozen ConvNeXt-L CLIP backbone, template prompts plus synonyms mapped to canonical labels, and fused in-vocabulary / out-of-vocabulary classifier scores with confidence filtering. It is optimized for Jetson AGX Orin using FP16, custom CUDA kernels for multi-scale deformable attention, an approximate softmax and vectorized top-k mask prediction, and runs at about 10 Hz on 640×480 RGB. It covers 560 object classes and 1306 text categories.

Semantic object mapping: SLAM Toolbox 2D pose-graph LiDAR SLAM with legged-inertial odometry produces an occupancy grid and pose. Mask centers are back-projected with stereo depth and intrinsics into the world frame, then associated or deduplicated by DBSCAN. Object positions are corrected on loop closure, and the map updates at 2 Hz.

Hierarchical scene graph: DBSCAN over object coordinates partitions space into areas. An onboard 4-bit LLaMA 3 labels each cluster as a room from its object list and a curated candidate room set. The result is a tree (floor/room/object nodes with level, label, instance id, location, parent/child) refreshed at up to 0.5 Hz.

LLM planner: GPT-4-Turbo (cloud API) receives the task, the JSON scene graph, feedback and action history. It outputs one of three primitives (goto(room/object), search_room(room), explore_globally) plus an explanation. It is called iteratively: a 360° scan first if the graph is empty, re-planning after each action, a 'Task done?' check after goto, and failure logs fed back as feedback.
Navigation: the ROS2 Nav2 stack uses cost-aware A* on an inflated occupancy grid for global planning and an MPPI local controller that outputs velocity commands.
Safety filter: a Control Barrier Function QP filter between MPPI and the locomotion velocity tracker uses raw LiDAR points to minimally modify commands for collision avoidance.
Exploration: the m-explore ROS2 frontier explorer uses frontier weight F_w = αF_d + F_n with α=50 to favor closer frontiers.

setting.backbone: GPT-4-Turbo (frozen, cloud API) as high-level planner; 4-bit LLaMA 3 (frozen, onboard) for room labeling; FC-CLIP with ConvNeXt-L CLIP (frozen, FP16-optimized) for open-vocab segmentation; classical Nav2 A*/MPPI + CBF-QP for control
setting.training_data: none (training-free; all neural modules are pretrained off-the-shelf models used zero-shot)
setting.observation: RGB-D from RealSense D455 stereo camera (640×480, 30 Hz) + top-mounted Hesai LiDAR + Unitree Go2 legged-inertial odometry
setting.action_space: high-level LLM primitives (goto / search_room / explore_globally) executed by Nav2 A* + MPPI + CBF filter as continuous velocity commands
setting.simulator: real world only (HM3D in Habitat used only to analyze VLFM under localization noise)
setting.privileged: none in main experiments (onboard SLAM pose, no GT map or semantics); in the dynamic-environment comparison, one of the two settings starts from a pre-built partial map

numbers_note: All results are real-world success counts; there are no standard benchmark (e.g., HM3D-ObjNav) results for OrionNav itself. The only simulation numbers (HM3D, 52.5% → 42.3% under injected noise) belong to the VLFM baseline and are excluded. Comparisons to VLFM and Clio are qualitative. Per-scenario percentages are given only approximately in the text ('approximately 88%', 'over 91%'), so only the exact success/total counts are recorded. The failure breakdown is described in the text and shown in a figure.
results: On a Unitree Go2 in four office environments, OrionNav completed 85/96 zero-shot real-world trials: 32/36 short-range object retrieval, 41/45 long-range object retrieval and 12/15 room navigation. None of the failures were attributed to the LLM planner or the scene graph. In dynamic-environment object search it succeeded in 9/9 trials (2–5 min each), versus 1/9 for Frontier-Search and about 56% for the Object-Map-Search ablation without room labels. VLFM could not complete the real-world tasks, and Clio could not run in real time on the onboard Orin.
limitations: Evaluation is small and custom: 96 real trials in office buildings, with no results on standard simulation benchmarks and only qualitative comparisons to VLFM and Clio, so cross-paper numerical comparison is not possible.
The high-level planner depends on cloud GPT-4-Turbo API calls, so the system is not fully onboard and needs network access.

2D LiDAR SLAM plus object-as-point representation limits geometric and 3D/multi-floor reasoning. Perception and localization errors (segmentation misses, SLAM/odometry errors, frontier exploration) remain the main failure sources.
